A Few Breaths in
the Grand Tetons

By Adriana Laura Cook
← Back to the Magazine

Five days, three lakes, and one quiet reminder that a life well-built is also a life well-lived.

The Teton Range doesn't ease you into it. Unlike most mountain ranges, it rises straight out of the valley floor with almost no foothills to soften the approach — one of the youngest, sharpest uplifts in the entire Rocky Mountain chain. Adriana traded five days of meetings, showings, and screens for a trip to Jackson Hole with her sister-in-law, chasing nothing more complicated than mountain air, slow mornings, and a little distance from the calendar.

Sunset over the valley, somewhere past the last soft roll of sagebrush flats.

The Company You Keep

The trip began the way the best ones do — with people, not plans. Adriana and her sister-in-law have the particular kind of friendship that grows sideways out of family, thirty years in and still easy. Five days with no meetings, no showings, and no reason to look at a screen turned out to be its own quiet luxury — not expensive in dollars, but in the courage it takes to actually put the phone down.

Mornings Belong to Persephone

Every good trip develops a ritual within forty-eight hours, and this one was Persephone Bakery — a whitewashed spot on East Broadway in Jackson known for its wall of wooden spoons, its wood-fired French pastry, and a James Beard semifinalist nod. They went early every morning for the croissants, eaten outside with the mountains doing what mountains do in the background — a small, reliable reminder that the highest form of luxury is often just something made well by someone who cares.

Persephone Bakery, East Broadway — go early, they sell out.

Delta Lake, and What It Asks of You

Then there was the hike. Delta Lake runs roughly eight miles round trip from the Lupine Meadows trailhead with about 2,300 feet of climbing — a generous first mile that turns, without warning, into six long switchbacks and a final stretch that isn't maintained by the Park Service at all. The last approach is an unofficial boulder scramble, hands involved, cairns as the only guide. What waits at the top is a lake the color of glacial turquoise, fed by rock ground to powder by the Teton Glacier above. The trail, Adriana writes, doesn't care who you are or what you've closed this quarter — it only asks one question, over and over: will you keep going?

The unofficial route to Delta Lake — hands involved, cairns as the only guide.
Delta Lake — the most impossible shade of turquoise, courtesy of glacial flour.

Taggart and Bradley: The Gentler Grace

The next day traded the exclamation point for the long, beautiful sentence: a comfortable five-to-six-mile loop from the Taggart Lake trailhead with only about four hundred feet of gain, winding through meadow, lodgepole, and glacial moraine to two still, mirror-like lakes. There was no destination to rush toward — just wildflowers, ambling, and stopping wherever anyone wanted to stop. A good life, Adriana reflects, needs both kinds of hikes: the one that empties you out, and the one where the destination is genuinely beside the point.

The gentler loop — meadow, lodgepole, and glacial moraine.

At the Table

Evenings ran through the old Teton Theater, reborn in 2017 as Hand Fire Pizza with its original marquee and ticket booth intact; a patio dinner at StillWest Brewery & Grill at the base of Snow King, dusty and sunburned and in no hurry to leave; and a Saturday night at The Bistro at The Cloudveil, a Parisian brasserie in spirit with a stunning zinc bar. Each one, in its own way, was a lesson in hospitality done properly — not the food alone, but the container it creates for people to be fully present with one another.

Five Days

Five days, it turns out, was exactly the right measure — long enough for the nervous system to finally believe you, short enough that you don't start unpacking your whole life into it. They came home on a Tuesday to find the inbox exactly where they'd left it. But something had shifted, and it hadn't shifted back.

“Go take a few breaths.” — Adriana Laura Cook
